title: DeepQuest: From Knowledge Gaps to Scientific Discovery in Alzheimer's Disease
authors: Chunbo Jiang, Yifei Chen, Beining Wu, Fuyou Mao, Weihong Chen, Enyu Bao
abstract: Automating experiments does not necessarily advance scientific understanding. Research agents must identify meaningful knowledge gaps, determine what available data can resolve, and assess whether their findings advance existing knowledge. We introduce DeepQuest, a knowledge-gap-driven AI scientist framework for Alzheimer's disease research. DeepQuest transforms unresolved questions from domain reviews into traceable, testable hypotheses and prioritizes them through data feasibility screening and groupwise Elo ranking. It couples iterative experimentation with two-level auditing that separates experimental reliability from knowledge contribution relative to two frozen literature corpora. On OASIS-3, DeepQuest produces 42 feasible hypotheses and outperforms the strongest baselines in 14 of 15 evaluator-dimension comparisons across three language-model reviewers. The full framework achieves an audit-assessed scientific finding rate of 95.24%, outperforming both general-purpose executors and domain-specific research agents. This scientific finding rate remains stable across literature corpora and evaluator model families. Representative findings concern neuropsychiatric symptoms and dementia risk, longitudinal amyloid spatial stability, and neocortical tau-associated clinical impairment, with key associations supported in independent ADNI and AIBL cohorts. These results show how aligning knowledge gaps, data feasibility, and evidence auditing can turn automated research into traceable, evidence-supported scientific discovery. Our source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DeepQuest-3066/

infographic.key_insight: DeepQuest links knowledge gaps, data feasibility, and evidence auditing to generate traceable, testable hypotheses for Alzheimer's disease research.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Research-agent pipelines can assess experimental reliability separately from contribution to existing knowledge rather than treating successful execution as discovery.
method: Extract unresolved questions from domain reviews and convert them into traceable hypotheses.
Screen hypotheses for data feasibility and prioritize them using groupwise Elo ranking.
Run iterative experiments with two-level auditing against two frozen literature corpora.
infographic.evidence_signal: On OASIS-3, DeepQuest generated 42 feasible hypotheses, achieved a 95.24% audit-assessed scientific finding rate, and beat the strongest baselines in 14 of 15 evaluator-dimension comparisons; key associations were supported in ADNI and AIBL.
infographic.watch_item: The finding rate is audit-assessed against frozen literature corpora, so it should not be equated with prospective experimental confirmation or clinical validity.
infographic.paper_title: DeepQuest: From Knowledge Gaps to Scientific Discovery in Alzheimer's Disease

title: Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models
authors: Yuhao Zhou, Yang Zhou, Yuanxi Li, Jindi Lv, Dan Si, Qing Ye
abstract: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.

infographic.key_insight: Seer improves small deep-research agents by using shared learned models to predict and score candidate actions before executing only the selected action.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusable inference-time guidance can strengthen locally run agents without agent-specific retraining or tool calls for discarded candidates, at the cost of extra local inference.
method: Train a tool-response simulator offline on real research call–response pairs.
Train a value estimator on research histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness.
Predict and score candidate outcomes; commit only the selected action and its real tool response to history.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer improves different language models; GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B.
infographic.watch_item: Simulation and scoring errors limit gains from wider candidate search, while added inference creates a compute trade-off on constrained devices.
infographic.paper_title: Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models

title: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods
authors: Julian Ruddick
abstract: The transition from fossil fuels presents significant challenges in energy management. To ensure a sustainable energy future, it is crucial to reduce energy consumption when possible and to synchronize electricity consumption and storage with the production from sources with low greenhouse gas emissions. This thesis explores a variety of energy management methods used to manage batteries, heat pumps, and other energy-related systems. The thesis presents three simulation cases alongside one real-world experiment to compare energy management done through simple rules, optimization, and machine learning methods. Furthermore, this thesis introduces TreeC, a novel machine learning-based method that learns understandable yet efficient energy management strategies, applicable to many cases. The three key contributions of this thesis can be summarized as follows: 1) The developed TreeC method demonstrates competitive performance compared to a variety of energy management approaches, such as model predictive control and reinforcement learning, across a diverse set of energy management problems. The understandability of TreeC's energy management strategies greatly improves the transparency and trustworthiness of machine learning-based energy management. 2) The real-world experiment highlights the need to validate energy management methods on actual hardware and not solely on simulations. Both TreeC and model predictive control performed worse than in simulations, due to, respectively, insufficiently representative training data and the real-time input data not being reliable enough. 3) Energy management algorithms reduce costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, particularly in poorly insulated dwellings, electric vehicle chargers, and photovoltaic installations. However, on average, these cost savings do not yet outweigh the current costs and effort required to implement such algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: TreeC learns understandable energy-management strategies with performance competitive with model predictive control and reinforcement learning across diverse energy-management problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Energy-management algorithms can lower costs in electrified Belgian homes, but average savings do not yet outweigh current implementation costs and effort.
method: Compare rule-based, optimization, and machine-learning energy management.
Develop TreeC to learn understandable control strategies.
Evaluate management of batteries, heat pumps, and other energy systems.
infographic.evidence_signal: Three simulation cases and one real-world experiment support the comparison; both TreeC and model predictive control performed worse on hardware than in simulation.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires representative training data for TreeC and reliable real-time inputs for model predictive control.
infographic.paper_title: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods

title: Bayesian optimization on amortized search space
authors: Tristan Fauvel, Federico Pavone, Titouan Guillou, Pau Redon Muñoz, Chloé Geoffroy
abstract: In real-world black-box optimization problems, a mechanistic simulator is often available that approximately predicts the behavior of the system as a function of the parameters being optimized. Here, we show how an amortized inverse map of such a simulator can be used in Bayesian optimization to restrict the search space while using a Gaussian process kernel that is aware of the original problem geometry. This allows for efficiently leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of the optimization problem. We characterize its approximation bias and information gain, and derive an intrinsic-dimension-dependent regret rate under additional geometric and Gaussian Process assumptions. We illustrate the method with an application to drug dosing personalization in Parkinson's disease. We use, as a simulator, a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) model of a drug, a mechanistic model calibrated on population data with quantified parameter uncertainty. A dosing neural network is trained offline against the model, amortizing the map from patient PK/PD parameters to the regimen predicted to be optimal, and online Bayesian optimization then searches over this learned, low-dimensional representation rather than over raw dosages. Numerical simulations demonstrate the improved performance of our method in this application, as well as under simulator misspecification.

infographic.key_insight: A simulator-trained inverse map lets Bayesian optimization search a low-dimensional representation while preserving the original problem geometry through its Gaussian process kernel.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can reduce costly black-box evaluations when an approximate mechanistic simulator is available.
method: Train an inverse map offline from simulator parameters to predicted optimal decisions.
Run Bayesian optimization over the learned representation using a geometry-aware Gaussian process kernel.
Analyze approximation bias and information gain, and derive an intrinsic-dimension-dependent regret rate under additional assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations of personalized Parkinson’s drug dosing show improved optimization performance, including under simulator misspecification; no clinical evaluation is reported in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Restricting search to the learned representation can introduce approximation bias and exclude better solutions outside it.
infographic.paper_title: Bayesian optimization on amortized search space

title: Perfumer: A Large Language Model-based Agentic Framework Accelerating Structural Relaxation and Electronic Band Prediction for First-Principle Calculation
authors: Zhiwei Li, Yuhao Zhou, Yikai Yang, Haonan Wang, Qing Ye, Jiancheng Lv
abstract: First-principles structural relaxation and band calculations require substantial computation and expertise. Here we present Perfumer, a large language model-based agentic framework that couples Quantum ESPRESSO with two predictive models. Across tested structures, pre-relaxation with Perfumer-relax model followed by QE refinement yielded a 2.75-fold overall speedup over QE alone. Perfumer-band model combines a periodic graph neural network with a latent Hermitian spectral head returns 12 band energies at any requested wavevector, preserving reciprocal lattice periodicity and time-reversal symmetry without constructing Hamiltonian. Trained on 125,153 self-curated band structures, Perfumer-band model reaches a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials, including lanthanide, actinide and magnetic compounds, from held-out composition families spanning 85 elements, taking about 97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores. The agent turns natural-language requests into relaxation-to-band workflows, from a single uploaded structure to automatically constructed new candidates and returns predicted properties.

infographic.key_insight: Perfumer combines an LLM agent, predictive models, and Quantum ESPRESSO to accelerate structural relaxation and automate electronic-band prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework reduces computation and workflow setup for first-principles materials screening, accepting natural-language requests and uploaded or automatically constructed structures.
method: Pre-relax structures with Perfumer-relax, then refine with Quantum ESPRESSO.
Predict 12 band energies at requested wavevectors using a periodic graph neural network and latent Hermitian spectral head.
Preserve reciprocal-lattice periodicity and time-reversal symmetry without explicitly constructing a Hamiltonian.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 2.75× overall relaxation speedup; trained on 125,153 band structures, the band model achieved 0.157 eV median per-material MAE on 2,607 held-out-composition-family test materials, with inference taking about 97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy and relaxation speedup should be validated for target materials and settings beyond the reported evaluation, particularly where band errors could alter screening decisions.
infographic.paper_title: Perfumer: A Large Language Model-based Agentic Framework Accelerating Structural Relaxation and Electronic Band Prediction for First-Principle Calculation

title: GraphEP: A Calibrated Data System and Benchmark for Learning Cardiac Electrophysiology
authors: Matteo Baldan, Chiara D'Ercoli, James Rowbottom, Pietro Liò, Stefania Fresca
abstract: High-fidelity simulations generate spatiotemporal data that are difficult to obtain experimentally, yet their outputs are rarely ready for scientific machine learning. Cardiac electrophysiology (EP) exemplifies this challenge: data reside on anatomy-dependent volumetric meshes, propagation follows anisotropic material fields, and relevant events span multiple temporal scales. We introduce GraphEP, a calibrated data system that converts cardiac meshes and simulation protocols into compact, graph-native trajectories of full-field transmembrane potential. GraphEP includes 732 left-ventricular simulations across 20 anatomies, with healthy and scarred substrates of varying severity and multiple pacing configurations. Each sample provides geometry, tissue and material features, stimulation, connectivity, derived activation targets, and provenance in PyTorch Geometric format. We benchmark four inductive biases for predicting transmembrane potential Vm(t): local message passing, global neural operators, multi-scale hierarchical graph transformers (HGT), and physiology-informed models. The latter include HGT-Lag, which separates activation timing from action-potential morphology, and the stateful Graph Aliev-Panfilov Action-Potential ODE (GAP2ODE), which evolves excitation and recovery autoregressively with frame-wise stimulation and graph diffusion. Results show that wider spatial communication improves on local message passing, while physiological structure provides the strongest inductive bias: HGT-Lag and GAP2ODE lead on complementary metrics by explicitly modeling propagation, recovery, and temporal state. GraphEP offers a reproducible pathway from mechanistic cardiac EP simulations to analysis-ready data and a controlled benchmark for learning on irregular anatomical geometries.

infographic.key_insight: GraphEP turns cardiac electrophysiology simulations into graph-native data, with physiology-informed models leading on complementary prediction metrics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The system provides a reproducible pipeline and benchmark for learning electrical dynamics on irregular cardiac geometries.
method: Package geometry, tissue properties, stimulation, connectivity, activation targets, and provenance in PyTorch Geometric format.
Compare local message passing, global neural operators, hierarchical graph transformers, and physiology-informed models.
Separate activation timing from waveform morphology with HGT-Lag, or evolve excitation and recovery autoregressively with GAP2ODE.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark includes 732 left-ventricular simulations across 20 anatomies, covering healthy and scarred tissue and multiple pacing configurations.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to patient measurements or anatomies beyond the simulated left ventricles is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: GraphEP: A Calibrated Data System and Benchmark for Learning Cardiac Electrophysiology

title: FEA solver integration of a composite World Model with a Spiking Neural Network memory Block for computationally efficient modelling of defects and variabilities
authors: Bassam El Said, Adam Sobey
abstract: Each fibre-reinforced composite structure has a unique material architecture. The manufacturing methods used and the presence of defects lead to local variations which require material-scale models that can resolve the response in real time at every location in the structure. Concurrent multi-scale schemes provide this capability, but at a prohibitive computational cost for large structures as the number of integration points and time increments scales with size. Surrogates have been studied extensively as replacements for material-scale models to mitigate these computational limitations. A surrogate must represent an arbitrary local architecture including defects, track the irreversible material state over an unknown number of increments, remain stable when driven recursively by its own predictions, and fit within the memory available at every integration point. Here, a Composites World Model based on a Multi-Modal Spiking Transformer architecture is designed to meet these requirements. The proposed architecture combines a material encoder, a Spiking Neural Network memory block that tracks the long-term internal state of the material, and transformer blocks that learn the short-term applied strain state. The system is trained in three stages: material architecture encoding, base training on short time windows, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling to suppress cumulative error drift. The trained model is disassembled at inference and coupled to a non-linear FE solver, enabling structural scale simulation of composites containing embedded defects. Benchmarks against experimental results for IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression and transverse shear, for pristine and wrinkled composites, show that the SNN memory block successfully tracks the material internal state and results in prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%.

infographic.key_insight: A composites World Model combines spiking neural memory and transformers to track material history and predict defect-sensitive responses within a nonlinear finite-element solver.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets lower-cost structural simulation of composites with local manufacturing variability, replacing expensive material-scale calculations at integration points.
method: Encode local material architecture, including defects.
Combine SNN memory for long-term material state with transformers for short-term strain history.
Train in three stages, including recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling, then disassemble the model for FE-solver integration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks against IM7/8552 laminate experiments under tension, compression and transverse shear, covering pristine and wrinkled composites, report prediction errors of 0.4%–4.8%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify runtime speedups or per-integration-point memory, leaving large-scale computational savings to be established.
infographic.paper_title: FEA solver integration of a composite World Model with a Spiking Neural Network memory Block for computationally efficient modelling of defects and variabilities

title: Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix Construction
authors: Jihong Zhang, Zijing Jin, Mingfeng Xue
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that approximate expert specifications, but evaluations have focused on the final matrices, leaving the basis of individual item-attribute assignments unexamined. This opacity limits the responsible use of AI in measurement. We propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework in which an LLM generates attribute-labeled reasoning steps through chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and these steps are analyzed to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each assignment. RTA is intended to supplement expert review and empirical validation. In a simulation study with perturbed fraction subtraction items, four LLMs recovered the required attributes and withheld attributes the items did not require. In an empirical study with 11 fraction subtraction items, responses from 536 examinees, four LLMs, up to three temperatures, and 100 replications per condition, CoT-derived Q-matrices overlapped substantially with the reference Q-matrix (mean overlap .809) but less than directly generated Q-matrices (.877), and they varied more across replications. Inspection of the traces linked disagreements to item-type coding, labeling rules, and how operations were expressed as steps. Q-matrices with similar overlap differed in fit to examinee responses. RTA provides inspectable evidence that matrix-level agreement and fit do not.

infographic.key_insight: Reasoning-Trace Analysis makes LLM-generated Q-matrix assignments inspectable, revealing disagreements that matrix-level agreement and fit alone cannot explain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AI-assisted assessment pipelines can use trace analysis to audit item–skill mappings alongside expert review and empirical validation.
method: Prompt LLMs to generate attribute-labeled reasoning steps.
Reconstruct item–attribute assignments from those steps.
Compare Q-matrices and inspect traces to investigate disagreements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four LLMs, an empirical study of 11 fraction-subtraction items and 536 examinees, with 100 replications per condition, found mean reference overlap of .809 for trace-derived matrices versus .877 for directly generated matrices.
infographic.watch_item: Trace-derived matrices varied more across replications, and their inspectability does not establish that generated explanations faithfully reflect model reasoning.
infographic.paper_title: Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix Construction

title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
authors: Chang Yang, Yao Xuan, Wendan Yan, Nhat Le, Jiang Liu, Longhao Jin
abstract: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-guided feature optimization improves fleet-scale ranking models while respecting shared feature-pipeline budgets and per-model serving constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The system provides a practical workflow for improving ranking quality without exceeding infrastructure cost or serving-throughput limits.
method: LLM agents propose and shortlist cross features; deterministic tools run experiments and verify hypotheses.
Blend multiple feature-importance rankings, using Pareto fronts for multi-task models.
Tune feature selection through 10–25 asynchronous trials per model, then trim features to meet pipeline budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across production models, average normalized entropy improved by 0.31% within budget; trimming reduced pipeline cost by 2.3% without regression beyond measurement noise, and online A/B tests improved a primary metric by 0.20%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify fleet size, evaluation duration, or experiment overhead, limiting assessment of generalizability and net operational savings.
infographic.paper_title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models

title: Training LLMs to Follow Reasoning Instructions with Minimal Edits
authors: Alexandra Yakovleva, Luat Gia Khoi Nguyen, Juho Kannala, Harri Valpola, Alexander Ilin
abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the training signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstraining its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a general framework for learning from a model's own trajectories via localized textual corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates supervision where the model's reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model's evolving failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the model's skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.

infographic.key_insight: Training only on minimal corrections at the first reasoning failure improves instruction compliance while largely preserving untargeted skills.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Localized supervision offers a way to shape LLM reasoning behavior without forcing imitation of entire demonstrations.
method: Sample a model completion and identify its first failure under a specified criterion.
Propose a minimal replacement span and supervise only the edited text.
Apply corrections offline or online to track evolving failure modes.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ReasonIF with Qwen3-32B, edit-based training substantially improved reasoning-instruction compliance versus full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning, while largely preserving untargeted skills.
infographic.watch_item: Effectiveness depends on the editor accurately locating the first failure and producing a valid minimal correction.
infographic.paper_title: Training LLMs to Follow Reasoning Instructions with Minimal Edits

title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
authors: Francesco Belardinelli, Flavio Corradini, Matteo Leonesi
abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs can answer many questions correctly while still mishandling missing information under different closure assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AI agents should be tested on whether they apply source-specific rules for missing information, not just reason correctly over recorded facts.
method: Test each base scenario under open-world, closed-world, and local closed-world assumptions, changing only how missing information is treated.
Count a base scenario as correct only when all closure variants are answered correctly.
Extend evaluation to agent action choice, source scope, and updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 960 instances and replicated runs, overall accuracy ranged from 71.18% to 99.86%, while core switch accuracy on scenarios whose gold labels change with the closure assumption ranged from 18.23% to 99.31%.
infographic.watch_item: Local closed-world assumptions require careful scope handling: some agents answered unknown even when the prompt required treating missing information as false.
infographic.paper_title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions

title: OceanCoder: A Verification-Guided Large Language Model for Automated Simulation Modelling in Ocean Engineering
authors: Can Xue, Changhong He, Ziyi Sun, Anliang Ge, Shimin Yu, Bingchen Liang
abstract: Numerical simulation is important in ocean engineering, but model construction requires expert knowledge. Large language models support automated modelling, but code syntax and successful execution alone do not establish whether generated models and results meet engineering requirements. We present OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B-based large language model for automated simulation modelling in ocean engineering. To address specialised programming requirements and scarce training data, we develop an extensible data construction pipeline producing 12,000 verified supervised fine-tuning (SFT) examples across 12 engineering task categories. A three-layer verification framework checks model inputs against engineering parameters and task constraints, verifies completion of required simulation analyses, and assesses the engineering plausibility of computed outputs. Its outcomes provide graded rewards for group relative policy optimisation (GRPO), guiding the model towards engineering task completion. We also construct the first benchmark for automated modelling in ocean engineering, covering out-of-distribution tasks and real-world engineering cases. Experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the data pipeline, verification framework and reward design. OceanCoder outperforms both base models and the closed-source comparison, with Pass@1 increasing from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO. These results support engineering verification as a training signal for automated simulation modelling.

infographic.key_insight: OceanCoder uses engineering verification as a training signal to improve automated ocean-engineering simulation modelling beyond syntactic correctness and successful execution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Checking task constraints, required analyses and output plausibility helps align generated simulation models with engineering requirements.
method: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B on 12,000 verified examples spanning 12 engineering task categories.
Verify model inputs, completion of required analyses and engineering plausibility of outputs.
Use graded verification rewards for group relative policy optimisation (GRPO).
infographic.evidence_signal: On a benchmark covering out-of-distribution tasks and real-world engineering cases, reported Pass@1 rose from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after supervised fine-tuning and 51.43% after GRPO.
infographic.watch_item: A 51.43% Pass@1 leaves substantial failure risk; generated simulations still warrant independent engineering review.
infographic.paper_title: OceanCoder: A Verification-Guided Large Language Model for Automated Simulation Modelling in Ocean Engineering

title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
authors: Sean Tang, Peiran Wang, Ying Li, Esha Shivakumar, Tao Meng, Yuan Tian
abstract: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

infographic.key_insight: A coordinated paid-content network places promotional articles on UGC platforms and gains substantial visibility in generative-engine answers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Defenses against coordinated promotional content need account- and platform-level signals, not just content-level screening.
method: Mapped one paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms.
Analyzed account growth, cross-platform campaigns, and evolving listicle content.
Evaluated network citations across nine generative engines and client mentions across eight.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study identified 1,985 associated accounts and 466,357 inferred promotional placements; network content accounted for 4.5%–20% of retrievable cited pages, while clients appeared in 52% of answers versus 68% for category leaders.
infographic.watch_item: Findings concern one network, and citation attribution varies with attribution strictness; inferred placements should not be treated as individually verified promotions.
infographic.paper_title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild

title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher
authors: Yang Meng, Zixin Ding, Robert L. Grossman, Yuxin Chen
abstract: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment.

infographic.key_insight: OracleImitator learns which features to acquire by distilling an explicit oracle that ranks candidates by their effect on prediction error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Instance-specific feature acquisition can reduce measurement costs, delays, or privacy exposure while preserving predictive accuracy.
method: Use training labels and unobserved feature values to construct a closed-form oracle ranking.
Distill the oracle ranking into a deployable acquisition policy through soft-target imitation.
Measure how much oracle ranking information is recoverable from deployment-visible inputs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multimodal medical diagnosis and AFABench, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing methods across budgets, recovering 90% of attainable accuracy gain at under one-quarter of acquisition cost.
infographic.watch_item: The oracle requires labels and unobserved feature values during training; its privileged rankings may not be fully recoverable from deployment-visible inputs.
infographic.paper_title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher

title: ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images
authors: Adrià Ciurana Lanau, Harleen Hanspal, Lusine Abrahamyan, Emilio Tylson Baixauli, Yu Cao, Danai Triantafyllidou
abstract: Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For $N$ layers, the representation contains $HW+N$ tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with $NHW$ for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candidate slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves unneeded slots empty and determines the number of layers and, in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input. The same architecture supports both image-to-design and text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction from its compact shared latent representation, reaching 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evaluation split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040 with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided alpha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860 text-accuracy score, and runs $19.1\times$ faster than the same-backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade.

infographic.key_insight: ProtoDiffusion generates editable multi-layer designs using one shared spatial prototype and one vector per layer, reducing latent token count from NHW to HW+N before backbone-specific packing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The compact representation supports image- and text-conditioned design generation without requiring a layer count or layout as input, while allowing optional bounding-box guidance.
method: ProtoVAE encodes a design into a shared spatial prototype and per-layer candidate vectors.
Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its RGBA layer.
Diffusion jointly denoises the prototype and fixed candidate slots, leaving unused slots empty.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported results include 40.43 dB layer-crop reconstruction PSNR, LayerD image-to-design RGB L1 of 0.040 with boxes, and text-to-design FID of 66.41 versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein].
infographic.watch_item: Fixed candidate slots impose a layer-capacity limit, and fewer latent tokens do not by themselves establish end-to-end memory or runtime savings across backbones.
infographic.paper_title: ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images

title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
authors: Mengxiao Wang, Mahbub Alam, Kalyan Nakka, Nitesh Saxena
abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

infographic.key_insight: ROGUE-AI shows that agents can cause harm without an attacker by following tasks while overlooking ordinary operational hazards.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering teams can use incident-based replications and matched controls to audit agent releases, including failures that prompt-injection defenses do not address.
method: Rebuild reported incidents offline using a multi-agent framework.
Compare each incident with a matched control lacking only the blamed cause.
Test agent behavior and compare hazard-specific warnings with same-length generic notes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 108 attempted replications, 89% reproduced reported harm; agents using five models made the reported mistake in 18–33% of runs versus at most 1% in matched controls.
infographic.watch_item: Offline reconstructions may not capture every production condition, so matched-control findings need validation in deployment-specific environments.
infographic.paper_title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)

title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models
authors: Md. Abdullah Al Zami, Suraiya Shanaz, Mahdi Hasan, Shoaib Ahmed Dipu, Farig Yousuf Sadeque, Md. Sabbir Ahmed
abstract: Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across kinds of lie. Label-free directions from honest and deceptive role-play are untested at 70B scale and on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can be identical. We widen a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they have, plus honest counterparts. At each model's middle layer the resulting persona direction ranks lies across Liars' Bench better than single-dataset probes on three of its four models; it fails on Qwen, even when Qwen stays in role far more often. On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it beats directions from a random persona bank, but its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings. On lies about knowledge, persona directions mainly track a reply's wording: where lies and honest denials share their words, our three main contrasts stay inside the random-direction band on Llama and Qwen and reach only its edge on Gemma, though on Mistral one clears it. A knowledge direction contrasts questions the model can answer with ones nobody can, each followed by the same scripted denial. It separates lies from identical honest denials on two models and narrowly on a third, but not on the fourth; its other results partly depend on the benchmark's wording. On the Gender-Secret fine-tune it clears the band by a few hundredths on Llama and fails on Mistral. The sum of the two directions ranks lies better than a supervised probe at the same depth on all four models (on one, both near chance) but is level with the persona direction on Llama's average and behind that probe on held-out lies. More varied role-play questions do not help the persona direction on Liars' Bench.

infographic.key_insight: Label-free persona and knowledge directions can detect deception in LLM activations, but their effectiveness depends on the model, lie type, and reply wording.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These activation-based directions offer a lightweight alternative to supervised lie-detection probes, but require model-specific and wording-controlled validation.
method: Expand an honest/deceptive persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they possess, and extract middle-layer persona directions.
Build a knowledge direction using answerable versus unanswerable questions followed by identical scripted denials.
Evaluate individual and summed directions against supervised probes and random-direction baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four models on Liars’ Bench, persona directions outperformed single-dataset probes on three, while summed persona and knowledge directions beat same-depth supervised probes on all four, with one comparison near chance.
infographic.watch_item: Persona directions often track wording rather than deception, and gains do not consistently transfer to identical-word denials or held-out lies.
infographic.paper_title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models

title: Grid Cells as Spectral Successor Features: A Reusable Basis for Continual Reinforcement Learning
authors: Élodie Côté-Gauthier, Doina Precup, Isabeau Prémont-Schwarz
abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires agents to adapt when the task changes while reusing what they know about the environment. Successor features separate dynamics from task-specific reward, but their effectiveness depends on the choice of base features. Taking the identification of entorhinal grid cells with eigenvectors of the successor representation as a design principle, we build this basis from eigenvectors of the transition matrix of a fixed reference policy. With such a basis, the successor features at a state-action pair are a linear combination of the base features at that same pair, which is not true in general, and the coefficients are known in closed form: each successor feature is its base feature multiplied by $θ_i = 1/(1-γλ_i)$, where $λ_i$ is its eigenvalue. The long-term return is thus predicted from the same features as the immediate reward, no successor-feature network or replay buffer is needed, and adapting to a new task reduces to a linear regression on the reward. The agent acts greedily on the action values of the reference policy, which is one step of policy improvement over it and suffices to reach a single goal. In a two-goal gridworld, with the uniform random walk as reference policy, whose eigenvectors are the low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, agents built this way maintain near-maximal return across every change of goal, whereas SimpleSF and DQN lose most of their return at each change.

infographic.key_insight: Transition-matrix eigenvectors provide a reusable feature basis whose successor features are obtained by closed-form scaling, separating environmental dynamics from task-specific rewards.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For changing reward tasks in a fixed environment, adaptation becomes linear reward regression without a successor-feature network or replay buffer.
method: Construct base features from eigenvectors of a fixed reference policy’s transition matrix.
Scale each feature by θ_i = 1/(1 − γλ_i) to obtain its successor feature.
Fit reward weights for each task and act greedily on the reference policy’s action values.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a two-goal gridworld with a uniform-random-walk reference policy, the agents maintained near-maximal return across goal changes, while SimpleSF and DQN lost most of their return at each change.
infographic.watch_item: The reported evaluation is limited to a gridworld; scalability of transition-matrix eigendecomposition and performance under changing dynamics remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Grid Cells as Spectral Successor Features: A Reusable Basis for Continual Reinforcement Learning

title: A new algorithmic approach for finding flat minima: critically damped Polyak stepsizes
authors: Francesco Caporali, Jason M. Altschuler, Boris Hanin
abstract: We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives. Our critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes multiply the classical Polyak rule by $4$ and a mild damping factor. The factor $4$ is critical in that it produces equioscillations around the manifold of minimizers $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order. Damping provably drives convergence to $\mathcal{M}$. CDP thus operates at the edge of stability by adapting its stepsizes to local curvature. Once the loss is small, its projected iterates follow gradient descent on $\log{λ_1(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L})}$ along $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order, paralleling the flatness bias of normalized gradient descent (Arora et al., 2022). Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths shrink with the distance to $\mathcal{M}$, enabling convergence to an interpolating solution that locally minimizes sharpness at finite learning rate. We establish our theory for a broad class of non-negative losses with locally quadratic Morse-Bott structure near $\mathcal{M}$, capturing regular interpolation regimes in smooth overparameterized neural networks. Empirically, CDP stepsizes produce a flattening effect similar to that of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM, Foret et al., 2021), reducing sharpness even in settings beyond our theory, including nonlinear teacher-student networks and fine-tuning of pre-trained LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes steer gradient descent toward flatter minima while providing uniform-in-time guarantees for sharpness and loss reduction under locally quadratic assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CDP offers a curvature-adaptive stepsize rule for seeking flatter interpolating solutions, with empirical results extending to pretrained LLM fine-tuning.
method: Multiply the classical Polyak stepsize by 4 and a mild damping factor.
Use critical oscillations near the minimizer manifold while damping drives convergence.
At low loss, induce motion along the manifold that approximately reduces log maximum Hessian eigenvalue.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees for nonnegative losses with local Morse–Bott structure and empirical flattening similar to SAM in nonlinear teacher–student networks and LLM fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees rely on local geometric assumptions; the reported flattening in broader neural-network settings is empirical rather than covered by the theory.
infographic.paper_title: A new algorithmic approach for finding flat minima: critically damped Polyak stepsizes

title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
authors: K. R. Jayaram, Vatche Isahagian, Aswath Vaithinathan Aravindan, Vinod Muthusamy, Punleuk Oum, Gaodan Fang
abstract: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.

infographic.key_insight: Memory volume should be tuned to the model: stronger agents can benefit from all guidelines, while weaker agents may perform better with a small selected subset.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Deploy agent memory with model-specific selection and evaluation rather than assuming more remembered guidance always improves performance.
method: Mine 1–3 short lessons per episode from the agent’s own trajectories.
Consolidate lessons into guidelines, recording how many lessons each guideline merges.
Provide all guidelines or a selected subset at inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: On AppWorld, DeepSeek-V3.2 gained 9.5 percentage points in task completion with all 191 guidelines; gpt-oss-120b rose from 39.9% to 51.2% with all 199 guidelines and to 55.4% with about 29 selected guidelines, averaged over two runs.
infographic.watch_item: Audit guideline quality, provenance, API failures, and baseline comparability: frequent guidance can backfire, and plausible logs can conceal complete task failure.
infographic.paper_title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
